CHERKASK, a town of Russia, in the country of the Don Cossacks, 36 m. ENE of Azof, and 276 NW of Georgiefsk, on an island formed by the Don and the Aksai. The houses are chiefly of wood, and a large proportion are built on piles, at a height of from 4 to 6 ft. from the ground, to protect them from the inundations to which the locality is liable from the beginning of April to the end of June. Viewed from the river, during the period of inundation, C. affords a novel spectacle. The entrance to it is by broad canals, and on each side the houses, built upon piles, appear to float upon the water; while the inhabitants pass between them in boats, or by narrow bridges formed by a couple of planks. When Clarke visited this town in 1800, it contained about 3,000 houses, and 15,000 inhabitants, a mixture of various nations, principally Circassians, Malo- Russians, and Russians, but also of Tartars, Poles, Greeks, Turks, Calmucks, and Armenians. C. was the cap. of the territory until the removal of the seat of government to New C.

CHERKASK (New), or Novo-Tcherkesk, a town of Russia, the cap. of the country of the Don Cossacks, on the Aksai, a tributary of the Manytsch, in N lat. 47° 21', about 54 m. This town was founded in 1806, at the recommendation of the hetmann Platoff; but it appears to have made little progress. Its buildings are chiefly of wood. A wide plain stretches along both sides of the Manytsch from C. to the borders of the Caspian, and is inhabited by various Calmuck tribes. A line of Cossack posts are drawn from this town to Lake Manytsch, and thence in a N direction along the borders of the government of Astrakhan.

NAMED AND AND AND AND AND AND AND AND AND AN CHO CHOCZIM, KHOCIN, or KHOTIN, a town and fortress of European Russia, in the gov. of Bessarabia. situated on a hill on the r. bank of the Dniester, 15 m. SSW of Kaminiec. It stands near the frontier of ancient Poland, and was formerly included in the Turkish province of Moldavia. Pop. in 1833, 9,869. The town was at first defended only by a castle; but in 1718 it was converted, by French engineers, into a regular fortress of great strength. C., formerly celebrated for several victories gained over the Turks by the Poles, in 1739 became remarkable for a great battle between the Russians and the Turks, which led to the surrender of the place to the former on the 31st of August. Being restored at the peace, it became again an object of attack in the following war; and, after another great battle gained by Prince Gallitzin, fell into the hands of the Russians, on 20th Sept. 1769, and remained in their possession till the peace of Kainarji, in 1774. In 1788 the united Russian and Austrian armies, under the prince of Cobourg, invested C., and having reduced the garrison by famine, forced it to surrender on 19th Sept. …

CONSTANTINOPLE,—the STANBOL, or ISTANBOL, or COSTANTINIYYEH, of the Turks, -a city of Turkey, the once splendid capital of the Eastern empire, and now that of the Ottoman empire, situated in 41° 0′ 12" N lat., and 28° 58′ 47" E long., on the sea of Marmora, and that deep inlet of the Bosporus known as 'the Golden horn,' at the extremity of a counterfort of a chain of high hills, which, running along the shores of the Black sea, the Bosporus, and the Propontis, joins Mount Hæmus at Rhodope. The formation of this counterfort on the S side is such that three-fourths of the houses of the city enjoy a noble view of the sea. Some large ravines, deepened by the rain, serve as outlets to the waters of the fountains, and divide the irregular base on which the city is built into several parts or hills, thus giving it a physical similitude to ancient Rome. Towards the land-side, or on the W, the city is defended by a ditch and a triple line of walls 4 m. in extent, the work of Theodosius II., flanked with lofty towers of various shapes, and pierced with six ivy-clad gates. The castle of 'the Seven towers' defends the point where the W wall meets that on the S side of the city. …

CORTETZ, an island in the Russian gov. of Iekaterinoslav, in the Dnieper, below the cataracts of that river, once the seat of the celebrated setcha of the Zaporogue Cossacks, and still exhibiting traces of their fortifications and camps. It is a natural fortress, rising more than 150 ft. above the river, and surrounded on all sides by granite rocks. It is now occupied by Prussian Mennonites, the descendants of the German colony founded in 1784 on the expulsion of the Zaporogue Cossacks to the banks of the Kuban.

txt: COURLAND, or Kurland [Esthonian, Kurama; SLAVONIAN, Kors, one of the Baltic provinces of Russia, comprising the duchies of C. Proper and Semigallia, and the districts of Pilten and Polangen. It is bounded on the N by the gulf of Livonia; on the E by the provs. of Livonia, Vitebsk, and Minsk; on the S by the prov. of Wilna; and on the W by the Baltic. Its outline is triangular, presenting its base or greatest breadth to the W along the Baltic; and gradually narrowing to its eastern extremity. Its length from WNW to ESE is about 210 geog. m. Its greatest breadth is 150 m. Its superficies is estimated by Hassel at 10,689 sq. m.; in the Weimar Almanach at 23.987 sq. versts or 10,627 sq. m. It is a flat country, interspersed with sand-hills, extensive heaths, and marshes, and patches of cultivated land. It is intersected by two ranges of hills running E and W; but the highest point, the Huningsberg, an alluvial sand-hill, attains an alt. of only 700 ft. The largest lake, the Usmaiten, is about 20 m. in circumf. The principal river is the Düna, with its tributary the Aa. The Windau and the Libau also intersect it. About two-fifths of the surface are covered with noble forests of pine and fir, intermixed occasionally with groves of oak. Agriculture and the rearing of cattle are the leading branches of industry. Corn, flax, hemp, and tobacco are cultivated. …

txt: TAURIDA, a government in the south of European Russia, between the parallels of 44° 26', and 47° 43' N; bounded on the N by the govs. of Kherson and Yekaterinoslav; on the E by the sea of Azof and the strait of Jenikale; on the S and W by the Black sea. It is composed of the following territories: 1st, The peninsula of the Crimea; 2d, a considerable track to the N of that peninsula, between the Dnieper and the Berda; 3d, the island of Taman or Tmutarakan; 4th, the land of the Tschernomorski or Black Sea Cossacks, lying to the E of the Crimea. All these, except the second, are described under their respective articles in the course of the present work. They are combined into one government, which takes the name of Taurida, from its principal part called by the ancients the Taurica Chersonesus. The superficial area of this prov. is 56,280 sq. versts, or 1163.38 German sq. m. of 15 to a degree; but the inhabitants are thinly scattered, their number being returned at 572,200 in 1846. This gov. contains some fertile tracts, particularly in the Crimea, but has also in its N part immense steppes extending to the Dnieper, the Kaskaia, and the Berda, many of them almost entirely unproductive, and all deficient in water, though others are covered with the finest grass. The summer is mild, but the winter, though short, is very severe. …

It has manufactories of wax and tallow candles, and dye-works. The district is to a great extent covered with bare mountains, and possesses little fertility. It is bordered on the SE by the Volga, and is intersected by several of the tributaries of that river. The rearing of cattle and the manufacture of pottery form the chief objects of local industry. The district contains one fown, 765 villages, 234 seignories, and 64,052 inhabitants.

txt: DAOURIAN MOUNTAINS, a range in Asiatic Russia, in the gov. of Irkutsk, between the parallels of 50° and 53°. This range passes to S of the Onon, and along the Argun. It is sometimes called the Nertschinsk mountains. Another chain running NE, and separating the tributary streams of the Lena and Amur, receives the general designation of the Daourian mountains. A little to the W of the sources of the Olekma, this chain takes the name of the Jablannoi mountain, or 'the Mountain of apples,' on account of the rounded shape of the blocks composing it. Acquiring increased elevation as it approaches the Eastern ocean, it begins, near the sources of the Aldan, to bear the name of the Stannovoi mountains, which afterwards gives place to the vague denomination of the mountains of Okhotsk, which are said to reach Behring's straits.

DMITROV, a district and town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. and 45 m. NNW of Moscow, on the r. bank of the Jakhrama. Pop. 3,000. It is illbuilt, but possesses an ancient cathedral, 5 churches, 2 of which are constructed of wood, a college and a convent, and has several manufactories of cloth, lace, leather, and porcelain. A fair is held once a-year. In the environs are the ruins of the palace of the counts Soltikov, which was destroyed by the French in 1812. This town owes its foundation to George Vladimirovitch, who, on his expulsion from the throne of Kiev in 1150, established himself in the locality. It subsequently became a frequent appanage of Russian princes, and suffered much in their feudal wars. In 1237 it was sacked by the famous Batu-Khan, and again in 1293 it sustained a similar calamity at the hands of the Tartar Dedene. In 1656 it was to a great extent depopulated by the plague.—The district comprises, in addition to the above-named town, 463 villages and 58,241 inhabitants. It is generally mountainous and woody, and is watered by the Jakhroma, Sestria, Dubna, Velia, &c. Cattle are pastured in great numbers on the mountains. The manufactures of the district, consisting chiefly in cloth, linen, leather, and soap, are numerous and extensive.

hier: Russian empire > governments of Voronetz and Saratof > governments of Saratof and Astrakhan > government of the Caucasus
txt: COSSACKS, or Kozaks, a military nation inhabiting the SW frontiers of the Russian empire, bordering on Turkey, Poland, Tartary, Siberia, and the Caucasian Isthmus; and constituting the principal defence against hostile incursions from these quarters. The origin of this people has never been satisfactorily ascertained. Some regard them as an offshoot of the great Slavonic stock; others are of opinion that they originally migrated from the Caucasian isthmus, and that they chiefly belong to the Tcherkess or Circassian nations. Others suppose them to have descended from the inhabitants of Casachia, a district lying between the sea of Azof and the Caspian, mentioned by Constantine Porphyrogenitus, a writer of the 9th cent. But, asks M. Hommaire de Hell, "is there any probability that the people of Casachia, after 600 years of absolute obscurity, and whose territory lay directly in the route of all those conquering hordes that, issuing from Asia, overran and ravaged Europe, and disappeared successively, should have again arisen out of the chaos of all these revolutions to produce the C. of our day? We have ourselves traversed those Russian deserts, up to the northern foot of the Caucasus; and except the somewhat modern remains of Madjar, on the borders of the Kuma, we nowhere found any vestige of human occupancy, or any trace of civilization. …

BIALYSTOCK, a province of Western Russia, which formerly constituted a part of the Polish waivodeship of Podlachia, but was incorporated with Russia in 1795. In 1807, a large portion of it was incorporated with the duchy of Warsaw, in terms of the treaty of Tilsit; and the remainder was erected into the prov. we are now to describe, which was placed under the superintendence of the governors-general of Grodno, and divided into 4 districts, named from the principal towns, Bialystock, Sokolka, Bielsk, and Drohiczyn. Its superficial extent has been estimated by Wiehmann, in 1813, at 158 German or 3,355 English sq. m.; and by Broemsen, in 1819, at 169 German or 3,589 English sq. m. The pop. in 1839 amounted to 227,106, of whom 31,376 were Jews. The greater part of this pop. are Catholics, of Polish-Mazovian descent. The surface is generally flat; and the soil light and sandy. Upwards of a seventh part of the surface is covered with forests. The principal river is the Western Bug. Its tributaries, the Nurzek and the Narawa, are considerable streams. The climate is temperate; but the great extent of marshy ground renders it, in many parts, unhealthy. Rye, wheat, buck-wheat, and flax are extensively grown; and the number of individuals engaged in agriculture was returned in 1830 at 198,502, or nearly five-sixths of the whole pop. …

W of the source of the Volga; runs through the W extremity of Lake Okhvat; pursues its course along the confines of the gov. of Tver, separating it from that of Pskov; crosses the NW point of the gov. of Smolensk, and makes a sweep of about 20 m. into the gov. of Pskov; then forms the line of separation between that gov. and those of Smolensk and Vitebsk; enters the latter, and passes Velij, Souraj, and Vitebsk, skirts the N extremity of the gov. of Moghilev; thence takes a NW direction, waters Polotsk, and forms the boundary line between Vitebsk and the govs. of Minsk and Courland, passing in its course Disna, Drissa, Drouia, Dinaburg, Jakobstadt; then runs along the S confines of the gov. of Livonia, separating it from the gov. of Courland; and, entering the former gov., throws itself, after a total course of 510 m., into the gulf of Riga, under the walls of Dünamünde, and 6 m. below Riga. The basin of the Dvina, which is of comparatively limited extent, is bounded on the NE by the Volkhonski mountains; and on the S and SE by a range of low hills, forming ramifications of the great ridge by which Europe is intersected. …

ELETZ, or YELETZ, a town of European Russia, in the gov. of Orel, situated on a hill in a beautiful plain between the river whence its name has been derived, and the Sossna, both branches of the Don, 115 m. ELKEN, or ITARALTSHIK, a salt lake in the Crimea, to the W of Mount Opuk. It is 27 versts, or about 18 m., in circumf.; and its S point appears to have formerly communicated with the Black sea. It deposits large quantities of salt.

SARATOV, or SARATAV, a government of Russia, situated between the parallels of 48° 5', and 53° 15', on both sides of the Volga, having on the one side the country of the Don-Cossacks, on the other the gov. of Astrakhan. Its surface is slightly undulated on the N and W; on the SE it stretches into immense plains. The Volga flows from N to S through the gov., and is skirted on the r. bank by a low chain of hills, which separates the basin of the Caspian from that of the sea of Azof. To the latter belong the rivers Karai, Khoper, Tersa, Medvieditza, and Ilovla. The basin of the Caspian is intersected by the low ridge of the Obshtshei-Syrt, which divides the valley of the Ural from that of the Volga. The rivers Sura, Tereshka, Sarpa, Maloi-Irghiz, Bolchoi-Irghiz, and Yeruslan, are tributaries of the Volga; the Bolchoi-Uzen and the Maloi-Uzen are affluents of the Ural. Though containing an area of nearly 75,000 sq. m., its pop. does not exceed 1,720,000. A barren soil and an unpropitious climate prevail in many quarters, while a great part of the tract to the E of the Volga is so impregnated with salt as to be in many parts unfit for the growth of plants. Of the numerous salt lakes in this quarter, the most productive is that of the ELTON: see that article. The country lying to the W of the Volga is less level, but has no hills of great height. …

txt: ELTON, or ALTIN-NOR, an extensive salt lake of European Russia, in the gov. of Saratof, circle of Kamyshinsk, 70 m. E of the Volga, and 200 m. S of Saratof, near the frontier of Asia. It is of an elongated form; its greatest diam., from E to W, is 13 m.; the smaller, from N to S, 10 m. Its waters are supplied by several small streams flowing from N and E, and being spread over a shallow surface estimated at 130 sq. m .- being in truth nothing more than a marsh lying above a bed of salt—the heat of the sun evaporates them, and forms the salt into a hard crust, which becomes several inches thick in the course of a season, leaving the lake in most parts dry. The pure material—a hydro-chloride of magnesia— finally obtained, amounts yearly to about 100,000 tons, and the number of workmen employed in preparing and transporting it is more than 10,000. The greater part is warehoused at Saratof.-Of all saltwaters that have been analyzed, that of Lake E. most resembles the water of the Dead sea. At a temp. of 54° its specific gravity is 1.27288.

EMBACH, a river of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Livonia, which issues from a small lake in N lat. 58°, runs SW, bends W, then N, and passes through Lake Virtzerv, issuing at the NE extremity, directs its course to the E past Derpt, or Dorpat, and falls into Lake Peipous. The upper and lower portions of this river, 36 and 42 m. respectively in length, are named the Little and Great Embach. It has a total course of 78 m., and is navigable to a considerable distance above Dorpat. Its principal affluent is the Aoua.

PIELISJAERVI, a lake of Russia in Europe, in the grand-duchy of Finland, NE of the gov. of Kuopio, and district of Karelensoefre. It is 75 m. in length from NW to SE, and 15 m. in extreme breadth. The Pielis issues from it on the S, and conveys its waters into lake Orivesi. Eno is situated on its S bank.

ENONTEKIS, a village of Russia in Europe, in the grand duchy of Finland, laen and 250 m. NNW of Uleaborg, near the shore and on the l. or E bank of the Muonio, in N lat. 68° 30', and at an alt. of 1,555 ft. above sea-level. A large fair is held here in the month of February, at which the merchants of Tornea exchange flour, salt, tobacco, coarse and fine cloths, hides, hemp, cordage, spoons, guns, axes, and hardware, for rein-deer skins, fox, hare, otter, beaver, squirrel, and ermine skins, dried pike, dried salmon, cod and stock fish, and butter. The sun is visible above the horizon here at midnight, during seven weeks of each year. The mean temp. is only 26°.85; but the mean temp. of the month of July is nearly 60°. A little barley is grown. The sunny season begins in May; and the * harvest is got in before the end of August, or even earlier. The most prolific return never exceeds sixfold. See on the subject of the climate of E. the 18th chapter of Prof. Thomson's Travels in Sweden. -The parish of E. has an area of 840 sq. m. Pop. 800, chiefly Laplanders, who employ themselves in fishing and the rearing of cattle.

ESTHONIA, a country of European Russia, adjacent to Livonia, and extending along the S side of the gulf of Finland. It now forms the gov. of REVEL, which see. E. belonged in early times to the Teutonic knights; and was afterwards an object of contest between Sweden, Russia, and Poland. The treaty of Oliva, in 1660, gave it to Sweden; that of Nystad, in 1721, transferred it to Russia, in whose possession it has ever since remained.

EUROPE EUROPE, One of the grand divisions into which geographers have divided the surface of the globe. Among these divisions, E. is that in which, while the works of external nature are on the smallest scale, the development of mind is on the greatest. Presenting an extent of surface amounting to little more than a fifth part of that of Asia or America, and a third part of that of Africa, and inferior in climate and native fertility of soil to a great portion of these regions, our continent shows that surface more crowded with men, improved by cultivation, enriched by productive industry and extensive commerce, embellished with mighty cities and splendid works of art, illumined with the reflections of genius, and invested with preponderance in the scale of political importance. In other regions we contemplate, amid the great physical features of the scene, A world of wonders, where creation seems No more the works of Nature, but her dreams. In E. we behold a yet more elevating spectacle,spirit asserting its supremacy over body,-and man, the lord of nature, pursuing most gloriously the high destiny originally assigned him "to replenish the earth, and to subdue it." In other regions it is matter we wonder at; in E. …

EVOUT'S ISLAND, a small island in the South Atlantic ocean, to the E of Wollaston island, in EVPATORIA, JEVPATORIA, or EUPATORIA, formerly called Koslev or Kaslof, and the Pompeiopolis of the Romans, a district and town of Russia in Europe, in the gov. of Taurida, 42 m. NW of Simferopol, on a bay of the Black sea. Pop. 9,460, chiefly Tartars and Jews. It is surrounded by walls now in ruins, and defended by an old fortress. It has several mosques, amongst which that built by Devlet-Ghiri-Khan in 1552 is a structure of great magnificence. There are also an Armenian and a Greek church, a synagogue, a high Tartar school, several medressehs, numerous khans or store-houses, a custom-house, 2 public baths, numerous coffeehouses, and an hospital. The port is small and shallow. The roadstead affords good anchorage, but, except on the N and NE, is destitute of shelter. It has, however, a considerable trade, consisting in salt, grain, bar-iron, wool, leather, cloth, skins, and butter. Quarantine is enforced upon all vessels coming from the Levant. The town is supplied with water by means of an artesian well. In the vicinity are two saline lakes, which annually afford an immense quantity of salt .- E. received its name from its founder, Mithridates Eupator, king of Pontus. Under the Tartar domination it was one of the most important and most populous towns in the gov. …
